content.prompt: Simplify. In this question, $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive and not equal to $1$.

answer.worked:
By the change-of-base product formula, $(\log_a b)(\log_b c)=\log_a c$.
$$\begin{align*}(\log_a b)(\log_b c)(\log_c a)&=(\log_a c)(\log_c a)\\(\log_a b)(\log_b c)(\log_c a)&=\frac{\log_a c}{\log_a c}\\(\log_a b)(\log_b c)(\log_c a)&=1\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Change to base $a$ and simplify. Assume $a>0$ and $a\ne1$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\log_a a^8-\log_a a^7+\log_a a^{11}&=(8-7+11)\log_a a\\\log_a a^8-\log_a a^7+\log_a a^{11}&=12\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$\dfrac{133}{60}$

Change each logarithm to base $a$, then simplify the fractional indices.
answer.worked:
Changing each term to base $a$ gives
$$\begin{align*}\log_{\sqrt a}\sqrt[3]{a}&=\frac{\log_a a^{1/3}}{\log_a a^{1/2}}\\\log_{\sqrt a}\sqrt[3]{a}&=\frac{1/3}{1/2}=\frac23,\\\log_{\sqrt[3]{a}}\sqrt[4]{a}&=\frac{\log_a a^{1/4}}{\log_a a^{1/3}}\\\log_{\sqrt[3]{a}}\sqrt[4]{a}&=\frac{1/4}{1/3}=\frac34,\\\log_{\sqrt[4]{a}}\sqrt[5]{a}&=\frac{\log_a a^{1/5}}{\log_a a^{1/4}}\\\log_{\sqrt[4]{a}}\sqrt[5]{a}&=\frac{1/5}{1/4}=\frac45.\end{align*}$$
The sum is
$$\begin{align*}\frac23+\frac34+\frac45&=\frac{40+45+48}{60}\\\frac23+\frac34+\frac45&=\frac{133}{60}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A culture of bacteria initially has a mass of 3 grams and its mass doubles in size every hour. How long will it take to reach a mass of 60 grams? Give your answer to the nearest minute.

answer.worked:
Let $M$ be the mass in grams after $t$ hours. The doubling model is $M=3\times2^t$.

$$\begin{align*}60&=3\times2^t\\2^t&=20\\\log_{10}(2^t)&=\log_{10}20\\t\log_{10}2&=\log_{10}20\\t&=\frac{\log_{10}20}{\log_{10}2}\\t&\approx4.321928\text{ hours}\end{align*}$$

The fractional hour is $0.321928\ldots\times60=19.315685\ldots$ minutes.

The culture reaches 60 grams after approximately 4 hours 19 minutes, to the nearest minute.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Write down a formula for $M$, the weight of bacteria in grams after $t$ days.

answer.worked:
The initial mass is 0.72 g and the daily growth factor is 5.

$$M=0.72\times5^t$$

Here $M$ is measured in grams and $t$ in days.

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is the weight after two days?

children.label: c
children.prompt: How long will the culture take to double its weight? Give your answer to the nearest minute.

answer.worked:
The doubled mass is $2\times0.72=1.44$ g.

$$\begin{align*}1.44&=0.72\times5^t\\5^t&=2\\t\log_{10}5&=\log_{10}2\\t&=\frac{\log_{10}2}{\log_{10}5}\text{ days}\end{align*}$$

In minutes,

$$\begin{align*}1440t&=1440\times\frac{\log_{10}2}{\log_{10}5}\\1440t&\approx620.17\text{ minutes}.\end{align*}$$

The culture doubles its weight after approximately 10 hours 20 minutes.

children.prompt: The mass of the Earth is about $5.972\times10^{24}$ kg. After how many days will the culture weigh the same as the Earth? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
Convert the Earth's mass to grams:

$$5.972\times10^{24}\text{ kg}=5.972\times10^{27}\text{ g}.$$

$$\begin{align*}5.972\times10^{27}&=0.72\times5^t\\5^t&=\frac{5.972\times10^{27}}{0.72}\\t\log_{10}5&=\log_{10}\left(\frac{5.972\times10^{27}}{0.72}\right)\\t&=\frac{\log_{10}\left(\frac{5.972\times10^{27}}{0.72}\right)}{\log_{10}5}\\t&\approx39.94\text{ days}\end{align*}$$

answer.short: The prediction is unrealistic: food and space are limited, so the bacteria cannot continue multiplying by five every day.
answer.worked: The calculation assumes that the culture multiplies by five every day indefinitely. Food and space would become limited and waste would accumulate, so this growth rate could not continue. The culture would not actually reach the Earth's mass after 39.94 days.

content.prompt:
The population of the People’s Republic of China in 1970 was 750 million. Assume that its rate of growth is 4% per annum.

For parts c and d, use the assumptions of question 3: the population of the Earth at the beginning of 1976 was four billion and grows at 2% per year. Give calendar years to the nearest year.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Write down a formula for $C$, the population of China in year $t$, $t\geq1970$.

answer.worked:
There are $t-1970$ years of growth, with annual growth factor $1.04$.

$$C=750\times1.04^{t-1970}\text{ million},\qquad t\geq1970.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: When would the population of China reach two billion?

answer.worked:
Using populations in millions:

$$\begin{align*}750\times1.04^{t-1970}&=2000\\1.04^{t-1970}&=\frac{8}{3}\\(t-1970)\log_{10}(1.04)&=\log_{10}\!\left(\frac83\right)\\t&=1970+\frac{\log_{10}(8/3)}{\log_{10}(1.04)}\\t&\approx1995.00794.\end{align*}$$

The model predicts 1995, to the nearest year.

children.label: c
children.prompt: With the assumptions of question 3, when would the population of China be equal to half the population of the Earth?

answer.short:
2014.

Equate China’s population model to half the world-population model and take logarithms.

children.label: d
children.prompt: When would everyone in the world be Chinese? (Discuss your answer.)

answer.short: The models predict 2050. This is unrealistic: as China forms a larger share of the world population, constant growth rates of 4% for China and 2% for the world cannot both continue.
answer.worked:
Equate the two model populations, measured in millions.

$$\begin{align*}750\times1.04^{t-1970}&=4000\times1.02^{t-1976}\\750\times1.04^{t-1970}&=4000\times1.02^{t-1970}\times1.02^{-6}\\\left(\frac{1.04}{1.02}\right)^{t-1970}&=\frac{16}{3}\times1.02^{-6}\\(t-1970)\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{1.04}{1.02}\right)&=\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{16}{3}\right)-6\log_{10}(1.02)\\t&=1970+\frac{\log_{10}(16/3)-6\log_{10}(1.02)}{\log_{10}(1.04/1.02)}\\t&\approx2050.08826.\end{align*}$$

The models predict equal populations in 2050, to the nearest year. This does not realistically predict that everyone would be Chinese. China is part of the world population; as its share increases, its 4% growth would push world growth towards 4%, contradicting the assumed constant 2% world growth. Beyond the intersection, these models would even predict China having more people than the world.

content.prompt: An amount of $\$80\,000$ is invested on 1 Jan at a compound interest rate of $7\%$ per annum. Interest is only paid on 1 Jan of each year. At the end of how many complete years will the investment first be worth at least:

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}A_n&=80\,000(1.07)^n\\110\,000&=80\,000(1.07)^n\\\frac{11}{8}&=(1.07)^n\\\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{11}{8}\right)&=n\log_{10}(1.07)\\n&=\frac{\log_{10}(11/8)}{\log_{10}(1.07)}\\n&\approx4.70677\end{align*}$$

Interest is paid annually. After $4$ years the balance is $\$104\,863.68$; after $5$ years it is $\$112\,204.14$. The investment first reaches at least $\$110\,000$ after $5$ complete years.

$$\begin{align*}A_n&=80\,000(1.07)^n\\200\,000&=80\,000(1.07)^n\\\frac{5}{2}&=(1.07)^n\\\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)&=n\log_{10}(1.07)\\n&=\frac{\log_{10}(5/2)}{\log_{10}(1.07)}\\n&\approx13.54285\end{align*}$$

Interest is paid annually. After $13$ years the balance is $\$192\,787.60$; after $14$ years it is $\$206\,282.73$. The investment first reaches at least $\$200\,000$ after $14$ complete years.

content.prompt: An amount of $\$120\,000$ is invested on 1 Jan at a compound interest rate of $8\%$ per annum. Interest is only paid on 1 Jan of each year. At the end of how many years will the investment first be worth at least:

answer.worked:
Let $A_n$ be the value after $n$ years.

$$\begin{align*}A_n&=120\,000(1.08)^n\\160\,000&=120\,000(1.08)^n\\\frac43&=(1.08)^n\\\log_{10}\left(\frac43\right)&=n\log_{10}(1.08)\\n&=\frac{\log_{10}(4/3)}{\log_{10}(1.08)}\\n&=3.738022\ldots\end{align*}$$

Interest is paid annually, so check the adjacent whole years:

$$\begin{align*}A_3&=120\,000(1.08)^3=151\,165.44\\A_4&=120\,000(1.08)^4\approx163\,258.68\end{align*}$$

The investment first reaches at least $\$160\,000$ after 4 years.

Let $A_n$ be the value after $n$ years.

$$\begin{align*}A_n&=120\,000(1.08)^n\\200\,000&=120\,000(1.08)^n\\\frac53&=(1.08)^n\\\log_{10}\left(\frac53\right)&=n\log_{10}(1.08)\\n&=\frac{\log_{10}(5/3)}{\log_{10}(1.08)}\\n&=6.637457\ldots\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Solve for $x$:

answer.worked:
The logarithms require $x>1$.

$$\begin{align*}\log_2\left(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\right)&=3\\\frac{x+1}{x-1}&=2^3\\x+1&=8(x-1)\\x+1&=8x-8\\7x&=9\\x&=\frac97\end{align*}$$

Since $\frac97>1$, the solution is valid.

answer.short:
$x=10$ or $x=10^{-5/2}$.

Use $u=\log_{10}x$ to obtain and factorise a quadratic.
answer.worked:
The logarithms require $x>0$. Let $u=\log_{10}x$. The power law gives $\log_{10}x^2=2u$ and $\log_{10}x^3=3u$.

$$\begin{align*}u(2u)+3u-5&=0\\2u^2+3u-5&=0\\(2u+5)(u-1)&=0\end{align*}$$

Thus $u=-\frac52$ or $u=1$.

$$\begin{align*}\log_{10}x&=-\frac52\quad\text{or}\quad\log_{10}x=1\\x&=10^{-5/2}\quad\text{or}\quad x=10\end{align*}$$

Both values are positive and satisfy the original equation.

answer.short:
$x=4$ or $x=2^{-5/4}$.

Use $u=\log_2x$ to obtain and factorise a quadratic.
answer.worked:
Since $x^3>0$, the domain is $x>0$. Let $u=\log_2x$. Then $\log_2x^2=2u$ and $\log_2x^3=3u$.

$$\begin{align*}(2u)^2-3u-10&=0\\4u^2-3u-10&=0\\(4u+5)(u-2)&=0\end{align*}$$

Thus $u=-\frac54$ or $u=2$.

$$\begin{align*}\log_2x&=-\frac54\quad\text{or}\quad\log_2x=2\\x&=2^{-5/4}\quad\text{or}\quad x=4\end{align*}$$

Both values are positive and satisfy the original equation.

answer.short:
$x=9$ or $x=27$.

Use $u=\log_3x$ to obtain and factorise a quadratic.
answer.worked:
The logarithms require $x>0$. Let $u=\log_3x$, so $\log_3x^5=5u$.

$$\begin{align*}u^2&=5u-6\\u^2-5u+6&=0\\(u-2)(u-3)&=0\end{align*}$$

Thus $u=2$ or $u=3$.

$$\begin{align*}\log_3x&=2\quad\text{or}\quad\log_3x=3\\x&=3^2\quad\text{or}\quad x=3^3\\x&=9\quad\text{or}\quad x=27\end{align*}$$

Both values are positive and satisfy the original equation.

content.prompt: Solve each set of simultaneous equations.

answer.short:
$x=3,\ y=5$

Express each equation with a common base, then solve the resulting linear equations.
answer.worked:
Using bases 3 and 2 respectively:
$$\begin{align*}3^{2x}&=3^{3y-9}\\2^{4x+4}&=2^{3y+1}\end{align*}$$
Equating indices gives
$$\begin{align*}2x-3y&=-9\qquad(1)\\4x-3y&=-3\qquad(2)\end{align*}$$
Subtract (1) from (2):
$$\begin{align*}2x&=6\\x&=3\end{align*}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{align*}6-3y&=-9\\-3y&=-15\\y&=5\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=5,\ y=2$

Express each equation with a common base, then solve the resulting linear equations.
answer.worked:
Using bases 2 and 5 respectively:
$$\begin{align*}2^{3x}&=2^{5y+5}\\5^{x-1}&=5^{2y}\end{align*}$$
Equating indices gives
$$\begin{align*}3x-5y&=5\qquad(1)\\x-2y&=1\qquad(2)\end{align*}$$
Multiply (2) by 3, then subtract (1):
$$\begin{align*}3x-6y&=3\\-y&=-2\\y&=2\end{align*}$$
Substitute into (2):
$$\begin{align*}x-4&=1\\x&=5\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=-\frac{63}{8},\ y=-\frac94$

Express each equation with a common base, then eliminate $x$.
answer.worked:
Using bases 7 and 2 respectively:
$$\begin{align*}7^{2x+6}&=7^{3y-3}\\2^{x+y}&=2^{3x-6y}\end{align*}$$
Equating indices gives
$$\begin{align*}2x+6&=3y-3\\x+y&=3x-6y\end{align*}$$
Rearrange:
$$\begin{align*}2x-3y&=-9\qquad(1)\\2x-7y&=0\qquad(2)\end{align*}$$
Subtract (2) from (1):
$$\begin{align*}4y&=-9\\y&=-\frac94\end{align*}$$
Substitute into (2):
$$\begin{align*}2x&=7\left(-\frac94\right)\\2x&=-\frac{63}{4}\\x&=-\frac{63}{8}\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=2,\ y=3$

Express each equation with a common base, then solve the resulting linear equations.
answer.worked:
Using bases 2 and 7 respectively:
$$\begin{align*}2^{3x}&=2^{2y}\\7^{3x+3}&=7^{3y}\end{align*}$$
Equating indices and simplifying gives
$$\begin{align*}3x-2y&=0\qquad(1)\\x-y&=-1\qquad(2)\end{align*}$$
Subtract twice (2) from (1):
$$\begin{align*}x&=2\end{align*}$$
Substitute into (2):
$$\begin{align*}2-y&=-1\\y&=3\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a rational-assumption contradiction and generalise it using unique prime factorisation; part b must also exclude integers containing only 2 and 5 with unequal exponents.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $\log_{10}3$ cannot be a rational number.

answer.short:
$\log_{10}3$ is irrational.

A rational value would give $10^p=3^q$ for positive integers $p,q$, contradicting unique prime factorisation.
answer.worked:
Suppose $\log_{10}3=\frac{p}{q}$ for positive integers $p,q$.

$$\begin{align*}10^{p/q}&=3\\10^p&=3^q\\2^p5^p&=3^q\end{align*}$$

The left side has prime factors 2 and 5, whereas the right side has only prime factor 3. This contradicts unique prime factorisation. Therefore $\log_{10}3$ is irrational.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that $\log_{10}n$ cannot be a rational number if $n$ is any positive integer that is not a whole number power of 10.

answer.short:
$\log_{10}n$ is irrational whenever the positive integer $n$ is not a whole number power of 10.

If it were rational, unique prime factorisation would force $n=10^k$ for a nonnegative integer $k$.
answer.worked:
Since $n$ is not a whole number power of 10, $n\ne1$, so $n>1$. Suppose $\log_{10}n=\frac{p}{q}$ for positive integers $p,q$.

$$\begin{align*}10^{p/q}&=n\\10^p&=n^q\\2^p5^p&=n^q\end{align*}$$

By unique prime factorisation, $n$ has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. Write $n=2^r5^s$, where $r,s$ are nonnegative integers. Then

$$\begin{align*}2^p5^p&=2^{rq}5^{sq}\\p&=rq\\p&=sq\\r&=s\end{align*}$$

Thus $n=2^r5^r=10^r$, contradicting the given condition. Therefore $\log_{10}n$ is irrational.

content.prompt:
Let $a>0$, $a\ne1$, and $x,y,z>0$. Prove that

\end{align*}$$
